passage:
Last year my senior, Sangeeta, presented my analysis to the leadership team as her own. A week later she waved away my next idea in a meeting with a smile. I felt heat behind my eyes. I said nothing in the room and could hardly hear the rest of the discussion.
That night I did not write an angry email. I made a folder with dated copies of my drafts, emails and versions. I spoke to two colleagues I trust, who had seen me work on it. Then I asked my manager, calmly, if I could present the next stage myself.
Nothing dramatic happened. But three months later my name was on the slide, and I slept better.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do with Abhinav's analysis?
qa.a: She presented Abhinav's analysis to the leadership team as her own.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling in the meeting when the next idea was waved away?
qa.a: Abhinav felt angry and hurt, described as heat behind the eyes, and stayed silent.

qa.q: What steps did Abhinav take instead of public anger?
qa.a: Abhinav kept a folder of dated drafts and emails, spoke to two trusted colleagues and asked the manager calmly to present the next stage.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have seen the situation?
qa.a: Sangeeta waved away the idea with a smile, so she may have seen it as a routine exchange and not known how much it stung.

grounding: A capable junior finds a senior credited for their work, and records contributions, seeks allies and stays calm.

passage:
Manager's note, written by Himani.
Zainab, a junior analyst, told me that the pricing model she built had been presented by a senior colleague without her name on it, and that a later suggestion of hers was brushed aside. She was upset but spoke evenly. She had already kept a dated record of her drafts and had talked to two teammates who saw her work.
What I did: I asked every contributor to present their own part at the next review and asked that slides carry authorship lines. Zainab presented the model herself. The senior colleague was quiet but did not object. Zainab told me afterwards that she had felt her hands shake and was glad she had prepared.

qa.q: What did Zainab keep to show her contribution?
qa.a: Zainab kept a dated record of her drafts.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when she spoke to Himani about the senior colleague?
qa.a: Zainab was upset and hurt by the missing credit but stayed even in her tone.

qa.q: What steps by Himani helped Zainab's work be seen?
qa.a: Himani asked every contributor to present their own part and asked for authorship lines on slides, so Zainab could present the model herself.

qa.q: How might the senior colleague have felt at the review?
qa.a: The senior colleague was quiet and did not object, so they may have felt awkward or caught out, though the note does not say.

grounding: A capable junior finds a senior credited for their work, and records contributions, seeks allies and stays calm.

passage:
In the Singapore office, Nkechi, twenty-five, spent three weeks building the market model for the regional pitch. Her senior, Mr. Lim, who barely understood the formulas, presented it to the directors as "my analysis." He didn't mention her once.
Nkechi's face burned. She wanted to stand up in the meeting and correct him.
Her colleague Mei caught her eye and shook her head slightly.
After the meeting, Mei said, "I know. He's done it to me. Don't fight him in public. Keep records: your emails, your version history, your notes. And send a thank-you note to the directors copying him, mentioning the model you built."
Nkechi took a breath. That evening she sent a short, polite email summarising her work on the model, copied to Mr. Lim and the director. The next week, the director asked her, not Mr. Lim, to explain the assumptions.

qa.q: How long did Nkechi spend building the market model?
qa.a: She spent three weeks building the market model.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling when her face burned?
qa.a: Nkechi felt angry and humiliated that Mr. Lim presented her work as his own.

qa.q: Why was Mei's advice wiser than public anger?
qa.a: Keeping records and sending a calm, polite summary made Nkechi's contribution visible without a fight, and it worked.

qa.q: How might Mr. Lim feel when the director asks Nkechi to explain?
qa.a: Mr. Lim may feel embarrassed, realising the director now knows who really built the model.

grounding: Outside India, a capable junior finds a senior taking credit for her work, and records, an ally and calm action work better than public anger.

passage:
At the government research lab in Hyderabad, Neelam, twenty-four, had found the error in the water-testing method that had delayed the project for months. Her senior, Baljeet Sir, who had been there twenty years, presented the fix at the department review as "the team's solution, which I directed."
When Neelam tried to add a point, he said, "Let the seniors speak, beta."
She went to the washroom and cried with anger.
Then she did what an older scientist had once advised her. She dated and saved every notebook page. She asked her colleague, who had watched her work late for weeks, to mention it in the next review. And she requested a short meeting with the division head, calmly presenting her data.
The division head listened carefully and asked her to present at the next conference. Baljeet Sir didn't speak to her for a week.

qa.q: What did Baljeet Sir say when Neelam tried to add a point?
qa.a: He said, "Let the seniors speak, beta."

qa.q: How did Neelam feel after the review?
qa.a: Neelam felt angry and hurt, crying in the washroom after her work was credited to Baljeet Sir.

qa.q: What made Neelam's response wise?
qa.a: She kept dated records, found a colleague as an ally, and calmly presented her data to the division head, instead of arguing in public.

qa.q: How might Baljeet Sir feel about Neelam's conference invitation?
qa.a: Baljeet Sir probably feels resentful and embarrassed, which is why he didn't speak to her for a week.

grounding: A capable junior finds a less skilled senior taking credit and dismissing her, and records, allies and calm action help more than public anger.

passage:
Dear Urmila Ma'am,
You were my mentor in college, and I need your advice.
At my new job, my team leader keeps presenting my ideas as his. Last week I suggested a new way to track shipments. He said, "Not practical." Two days later he presented it to the manager as his plan. The manager praised him.
I was so angry I wanted to email the whole team. I didn't. I remembered you saying, "Anger is a message, not a strategy."
So I've started keeping a record: every idea, with the date I sent it. I've found one colleague who saw it happen and is willing to speak if needed. And next week, I'll ask the manager for a short one-on-one to walk through my plan's details, which my team leader doesn't know.
Does that sound right? I don't want to fight. I want to be seen fairly.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Lakshmi suggest last week?
qa.a: Lakshmi suggested a new way to track shipments.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when the team leader presented Lakshmi's idea as his?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt so angry that she wanted to email the whole team.

qa.q: What steps is Lakshmi taking, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Lakshmi is keeping a dated record of the ideas, finding an ally who saw it, and asking the manager for a one-on-one, which is calmer and more effective than public anger.

qa.q: How might Urmila Ma'am feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Urmila Ma'am would likely feel proud that Lakshmi remembered her advice and chose a calm strategy.

grounding: A capable junior whose senior takes credit for her ideas chooses to record contributions, find allies and stay calm rather than show public anger.

passage: I'll tell you what happened with the client deck, because I'm still a bit proud of how I handled it. I'm Bidisha. I built the whole market analysis for the Pune client: three weeks, every chart. In the review, my senior, Mr. Ghosh, presented it as his team's work and didn't say my name once. When I suggested a better pricing slide, he waved it away: "Let's keep it simple." My ears were ringing. I wanted to stand up and say, "That's mine." I didn't. That evening I started a simple log: what I did, the dates, the files with my name in the version history. Trisha from strategy had seen my drafts, and she said she'd back me. Two weeks later, at my quarterly talk, I showed the log to our department head, calmly, no drama. She said, "Thank you, I didn't know." On the next client, my name is on the cover.

qa.q: How long did Bidisha spend on the market analysis?
qa.a: Bidisha spent three weeks on it.

qa.q: What did Bidisha feel when Mr. Ghosh presented the work as his team's?
qa.a: Bidisha felt angry and hurt, with ears ringing and an urge to stand up and claim it.

qa.q: Which steps helped Bidisha more than public anger would have?
qa.a: Keeping a dated log with version history, getting Trisha's support, and calmly showing it to the department head at a quarterly talk.

qa.q: How might the department head see Bidisha after the log?
qa.a: The head seems grateful and newly aware of Bidisha's work, which is why Bidisha's name is on the next cover.
